newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt hurt by sleaze factor in pre-Budget vacuum.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt hurt by sleaze factor in pre-Budget vacuum.

text.p: A series of minor scandals is threatening the unity of New Zealand's centre-right coalition government and damaging its public image as it prepares its first budget, due on June 26.

The Labour opposition has seized on the government's political embarrassments, some of which involve the Deputy Prime Minister, following the successful use of the "sleaze factor" by its British counterpart against the Conservative party in Britain.

Opinion polls now put Labour and the main government party, the conservative National Party, neck-and-neck seven months after an election which saw National cling to office by striking a coalition deal with nationalist New Zealand First.
Over the same period, NZ First has fared worse, falling from 13 percent at the polling booth to just five percent support.
Flamboyant Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters, who is also NZ First's leader, blames the media for blowing "sideshows" out of proportion.

"If you read the newspapers and watch television and listen to the radio, you could be forgiven for thinking the government was in the middle of an Italian style meltdown, with the coalition on its knees, bloody and bruised," Peters told a business audience on Tuesday.
He said despite criticisms from some parts of National, NZ First would stick to the coalition agreement for three years.
However, some of the government's worst credibility worries stem from NZ First MPs, including Peters.

Two have been accused in the media of misspending public money. Last week Parliament's powerful privileges committee deemed Peters had technically assaulted a fellow government MP by restraining him against his will, and of unbecoming conduct.
That committee included Prime Minister Jim Bolger and Attorney-General Paul East, a senior National frontbencher.
Peters' refusal to accept its advice and apologise to parliament has also undermined relations within the government.
National Party president Geoff Thompson has spoken of ruling out a joint campaign at the next election.
On Saturday, Parliament's speaker and National MP Doug Kidd said unless there was a miracle "we probably won't know them (NZ First) on the day after we adjourn the House for the 1999 election".
"Most folk in NZ First hate what's happening to them. Most are desperate to find a way out. If they do not they are dog tucker (dogmeat) in 1999," Kidd said.
Lobbyist and public relations consultant Roger Mackey, a former press secretary to Finance Minister Bill Birch, said the government was running smoothly but for the irritating scandals.
"But it is hard to establish an action plan in public because Winston Peters has gone for the big bang in the budget."
Since 1991, when National was mauled after a surprisingly radical budget, ministers have been more cautious.
Government strategists say Peters desperately wants a showcase budget to demonstrate he has been able to loosen the government's purse-strings, and make his party's presence felt.
But major surprises are unlikely as the December coalition agreement set a limit on extra spending of NZ$5 billion ($3.46 billion) over three years and defined major policy planks.
